title: Routing, risk labels and live metrics

story: On Monday morning Byte, our review agent, reviews two PRs. The first fixes a typo in a README: two changed lines. The second changes the permission check that decides who may read a dataset. Byte gives both exactly the same review: Opus 5.5 at high effort, about five minutes and two dollars each, one comment window, nothing that tells the human reviewer which of the two deserves their full attention.

That is wasteful at one end and thin at the other. The typo needed a quick look. The permission change deserved more than our normal review, and its reviewer should have been warned before they opened it.
hook.question: How does Byte decide, from the files a PR changes, how hard to look and how loudly to warn?

read.h: A route: how hard to look
p: Effort is the setting that tells Claude how much to reason before it answers. More effort means more thinking tokens, more minutes and more money, and often better answers on hard problems. Byte uses high effort on every review today, because that was the safe default. But Anthropic measured medium effort matching the old high on many tasks at about half the tokens, and a README typo needs even less.

So Byte's gate now chooses a route for each review: a model, an effort and a reason, computed from the PR's changed files. Size is additions plus deletions, without lockfiles and generated files, because a 4,000-line package-lock.json says nothing about how risky a change is. If every counted file is documentation, or every file is a test, or every file is a dependency list, the review runs at low. A big PR, over 400 changed lines, keeps high. Everything else gets medium. The model stays Opus 5.5 for all of them; only the effort moves. A team that sets its own model in Byte's policy still wins over the route.

notes.text: Lockfiles and generated gRPC code: left out of the count, and never decide the kind.
every() on the counted files: a PR is docs-only only if all of them are docs.
Docs-only, test-only or dependency-only: low effort, whatever the size.
Over 400 counted lines: keep today's high effort.

read.h: A route must earn its place
p: A cheaper route is a guess until BYTE-GOLD says otherwise. Each route is replayed on its slice of the dev cases: the docs-only cases at low, the ordinary ones at medium. It stays only if its recall on high bugs is within 3 points of what high effort catches on the same cases, and clean PRs get no more false alarms. A route that loses returns to high. The change itself ships through the gate from the replay lesson, like any change to Byte's model or effort.

The plumbing is small. The gate gets a new output, effort, next to the model it already returns. The review workflow passes it to the worker as --effort, and the worker uses it instead of the constant it uses today. The route and its reason appear on Byte's dashboard and in its status comment, so anyone can see why a review was light.

read.h: A risk label: where the reviewer should look
p: Every fcp PR gets exactly one human approval. For that one reviewer, it matters a lot whether a PR touches a database migration, the permission checks or the contract between the cloud and the on-prem client. So Byte gives every PR a label, risk:low, risk:med or risk:high, and a check named Byte risk that lists the reasons. High comes from a list of paths agreed with the frontend and backend guilds, our groups of product engineers. Low means every file is documentation, a Storybook story or a test. Everything else is med, and a PR over 800 changed lines is raised one level.

Two choices keep the label honest. First, the tiers live in Byte's own policy file, which is built into Byte's signed image, and never in a file inside fcp. If they lived in fcp, a PR could edit them and lower its own tier. Second, the label informs and never decides: the check's result is neutral (neither green nor red), it is not a required check, and it never changes who may approve or how many approvals a PR needs.

notes.text: The tiers are policy, read from Byte's image. A PR to fcp cannot change them.
Low only if every file matches a low path; otherwise start at med.
One file on a high path makes the whole PR high.
Size raises the tier one step, so a huge ordinary PR gets a warning too.

read.h: Deep mode only where a miss hurts
p: Byte also has a much heavier way to review, the panel: five separate review sessions, each looking for one kind of problem (one lens), and then a skeptic that tries to disprove every finding. The last lesson of this part builds it. Reviews like that cost roughly $15 to $25 per PR at list price, against about $2 for Byte today, so they belong only on the PRs where a missed bug hurts most.

reviewMode uses the risk tier for that. A risk:high PR, a PR over 800 changed lines, or a comment @byte-review deep runs the panel; every other PR keeps today's single session. Both paths end in the same review and the same check run, so nothing else changes. Before deep mode runs on real PRs, both modes are replayed on BYTE-GOLD and compared on recall, false alarms, cost and minutes. Deep mode ships for risk:high only if it does not lower recall on high bugs and keeps clean false alarms at 0.2 per PR or less.

notes.text: A person can always ask for the panel on one PR.
The risk label from the previous section decides the expensive review too.

deeper.h: Go deeper: do people act on Byte at all?
p: BYTE-GOLD tells us whether a change makes Byte better or worse on a fixed set. It cannot tell us whether people act on Byte's comments in real PRs, which is the whole point of a reviewer. So Byte's weekly job gives each finding on a merged PR a fate. A finding is addressed when a later sniff called it fixed and sure, or when GitHub shows the comment as outdated at merge because the code under it changed (a rebase can also outdate a comment, so the sniff is the stronger signal). A reply alone does not count. A finding is wrong when someone with write access gave it a thumbs-down.

The targets are at least 65% of high findings addressed and under 3% marked wrong. Each month there is also live recall: run the miner from the first lesson of this part (the script that finds which PR introduced each fixed bug) on last month's fixed bugs, and check whether Byte had flagged the bug on the PR that introduced it. The rows hold ids, severities and fates only, never paths or text, and the nightly metrics job turns them into dashboards per team.

lab.title: Route five PRs
lab.goal: Write the route, the risk tier and the review mode as one small module, run it on five PRs, and find the PR that the plan's version sends to the expensive panel by mistake.

guess.q: A PR from Renovate, the bot that opens dependency updates, changes frontend/package.json (2 lines) and frontend/package-lock.json (4,000 lines). Which effort does reviewRoute choose?

options.text: high, because 4,002 lines is far over 400
options.why: The lockfile is left out of the count and out of the kind, so the PR is 2 lines of package.json.

options.text: low, because after leaving out the lockfile every file is a dependency list
options.why: GENERATED drops the lockfile, and the only file left matches DEPS.

options.text: medium, because it is not docs or tests
options.why: Dependency-only is the third low-effort kind, next to docs-only and test-only.

follow.say: Write the three decisions as one module. It is the code from the Understand step with the policy written inline and Node's matchesGlob instead of Byte's helper.
Describe five PRs by their changed files and print what Byte would do with each.

lab.build: Write more.ts with two new PRs and predict each row before you run it: a Storybook-only PR (frontend/src/components/ProjectsTable/ProjectsTable.stories.tsx, 120 added lines) and a CI change (.github/workflows/frontend-ci.yml, 6 added and 4 removed). Then print reviewMode("low", 2, "deep"). Explain why the Storybook PR is risk:low but still gets medium effort.

lab.fix: Bump zod, a PR from Renovate (the bot that opens dependency updates) that changes one line of package.json and 4,000 lines of package-lock.json, is labelled risk:high and sent to deep mode: about $20 of panel review for a version bump. reviewRoute leaves the lockfile out of its count, but riskFor (and the line count passed to reviewMode) do not. Export GENERATED from route.ts, filter it out of the line count in riskFor and in prs.ts, and run node prs.ts again: Bump zod should become risk:med and standard.
explain: Why are lockfiles left out when Byte measures the size of a PR?
Why do the risk tiers live in Byte's policy and not in a file inside fcp?
The risk label never changes who may approve. Then what is it for?
lab.done: Your table shows Bump zod as risk:med and standard, and you can say why each of the other PRs got its effort, tier and mode.

check.q: A PR changes three Markdown files and frontend/package-lock.json, 4,000 lines in all. Which effort does the route pick?

options.text: low, because after leaving out the lockfile every file is documentation
options.why: Generated files never count and never decide the kind, so this is a docs-only PR.

options.text: high, because the PR is over 400 lines
options.why: The 4,000 lines are the lockfile, which is left out of the count.

options.text: medium, because a lockfile is neither docs nor tests
options.why: The lockfile is filtered out before the kind is checked.

check.q: Why do fcp's risk tiers live in Byte's policy, baked into its image, instead of a file in fcp?

options.text: Byte cannot read files from the repo it reviews
options.why: It reads the PR's files all the time. The point is who can change the rules.

options.text: So that a PR cannot edit the rules and lower its own tier
options.why: A rule file in fcp could be changed in the same PR it judges. Rules from the reviewed repo are untrusted data.

options.text: Because the tiers change on every release of Byte
options.why: They change rarely, through a reviewed PR to Byte. Where they live is about trust, not speed.

check.q: A PR touches cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/permissions.py and gets risk:high. What changes for that PR?

options.text: It needs two approvals instead of one
options.why: The label never changes the approval rules: one approval, never by the requester, for every PR.

options.text: Byte's risk check fails until a security reviewer approves
options.why: The check is neutral and not required. It informs; it never blocks.

options.text: The reviewer sees the label and its reason, and Byte reviews it in deep mode with the panel
options.why: The tier tells the one reviewer where to look and decides that Byte spends more effort on it.

p: In RhinoHealth/byte: src/route.ts (reviewRoute, later reviewMode), additions and deletions on PullRequestFile in src/types.ts, a new effort output from gate(), --effort "$EFFORT" in review.yml, an optional --effort in cli.ts with CLAUDE_EFFORT as the default, and engines.ts using it. claude-sonnet-5-5 joins SUPPORTED_MODELS for the panel's conventions lens; reviews stay on Opus 5.5. Each route is proved on its BYTE-GOLD dev slice and ships through the gate; Nave reviews it.

Risk: a risk block per repository in config/repositories.json, src/risk.ts, a risk subcommand that sets one label and a completed neutral Byte risk check run, a reusable risk.yml in Byte and a new caller byte-risk.yml in fcp on opened, reopened, synchronize and ready_for_review (a separate file, because adding opened to byte-review.yml would start a full review on every new PR). The three labels are created once with gh label create; the check is never added to the ruleset. riskFor should leave lockfiles and generated files out of its line count, as reviewRoute does, or every large Renovate PR becomes risk:high and runs the panel. Live metrics: finding fates from the weekly-harvest stage in src/weekly.ts, merged into data/finding-fates.jsonl, and byte_findings_addressed_ratio, byte_findings_wrong_ratio and byte_live_recall in VictoriaMetrics.

tickets.why: The route: model and effort per PR from size and kind, each route proved on BYTE-GOLD.
risk:low, med or high on every fcp PR, with a neutral check and the reasons.
Deep mode for risk:high, large PRs and @byte-review deep, after measuring cost and quality.
Live numbers: addressed rate, wrong rate and monthly live recall.

words.plain: The setting that decides how much Claude reasons before answering: low, medium or high.
The model, effort and reason Byte's gate picks for one review from the PR's files.
risk:low, risk:med or risk:high, from the paths a PR touches and its size.
A check run that shows information and is neither green nor red; it never blocks a merge.
Byte's expensive review: five lenses and a skeptic, used only where a miss hurts most.
What happened to one Byte finding on a merged PR: addressed or open, and whether people marked it wrong.

review.q: From memory: the three kinds of PR that get low effort, and the size that keeps high.
review.a: Docs-only, test-only and dependency-only PRs get low; over 400 changed lines (lockfiles and generated files left out) keeps high; everything else is medium.

review.q: What has to be true before a cheaper route stays in Byte?
review.a: On its BYTE-GOLD dev slice, recall on high bugs within 3 points of high effort, and no more false alarms on clean PRs. Otherwise the route goes back to high.

review.q: Name the three ways a PR gets deep mode.
review.a: It is risk:high, it has more than 800 changed lines, or someone comments @byte-review deep.

remember: Let the changed files decide the review: effort from size and kind, a risk label that informs the one reviewer, and the expensive panel only where a missed bug hurts most.
